findings: characters-counted-as-bytes (severity 3): the tool counts characters as UTF-8 bytes, where its specification defines them as Unicode code points.
words-split-at-white-space (severity 3): the tool splits words at white space, where its specification defines a word as a run of letters, digits, apostrophes and hyphens.
gain: Both counting faults share one cause: the counting function, which returns (lines, words, characters), uses language stand-ins (split at white space for words, the UTF-8 byte length for characters) instead of the specification's definitions. Counting by the definitions themselves fixes 6 of the 18 use cases: 5 move from grade 0.1 to 1.0 and the use case on words with non-ASCII letters moves from 0.7 to 1.0. The grade total rises from 12.9 to at least 17.7 of 18.
delta: None. The specification already defines Words and Characters; the prototype departs from them. The one choice the specification leaves open, that a combining mark belongs to the word it follows, is recorded as one line in the project's record of open choices.
design: The counting function counts characters as the number of code points. It counts words as runs of characters that are letters (Unicode category L*), digits (N*), apostrophes or hyphens, with a combining mark (M*) joining the run it follows, using the standard library's Unicode database. One test per definition, with non-ASCII text. Released as prototype version 0.3.

context: The tool reads a text on standard input and prints its lines, words and characters, or only its words; Python 3.9, standard library only. Version 0.0 is the first prototype; each change is one version and one commit. Each of 18 use cases is a run of the tool graded from 0 to 1 by how well its output meets the specification; the grade total is their sum.

pattern.context: A component is built from a specification that defines its terms, such as what counts as a word or a character.
pattern.problem: The code uses a built-in that approximates a definition, such as splitting at white space or taking a byte length. On plain ASCII test text the built-in and the definition agree, so the tests pass and several faults share one hidden cause.
pattern.solution: Implement the definition itself. Record any edge choice the specification leaves open. Test each definition with input on which the built-in and the definition disagree, such as non-ASCII text and punctuation without spaces.
pattern.consequences: One change closes every fault with that cause and adds tests that would catch its return. The code is a little longer and may run slower than the built-in.
